To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

expert interventionists produce greater behavior change than community members; that the demographic and behavioral characteristics of the interventionist and recipient influence the effectiveness of the intervention; and that these effects are moderated by the social and economic status of the recipients.

experts are more effective interventionists than lay community members and that interventionists who are similar to recipients are more effective than dissimilar interventionists, but only when recipients are low in power or status.

the effects of HIV prevention interventionists on the behavior of their target populations depend on the social status and power of the recipients, as well as the similarity between the recipients and the interventionists.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social agents of behavior change.
the influence of social agents of behavior change on HIV prevention, and the implications of these findings for the design, implementation, and evaluation of interventions.
the role of social agents in facilitating behavior change, and the ways in which the characteristics of the interventionist affect the outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
experts, lay community, and dissimilar others are more effective than similar others in changing behavior, especially among populations with lower status and/or power.
the social agents of behavior change have differential effects on different groups, and these effects can be predicted by theoretical models of social influence.
experts are more effective than lay community members and that the effectiveness of both is enhanced by demographic and behavioral similarity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effectiveness of social agents of behavior change depends on the nature and characteristics of the intervention, the interventionists, and the recipients. (author abstract)
the social agents of behavior change can be a powerful force in the process of HIV-prevention.
the effectiveness of HIV-prevention interventions depends not only on their content but also on the social agents of change.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the characteristics of the agent of change can influence the effectiveness of the intervention.
the social context of HIV prevention interventions is an important determinant of their effectiveness.

there are many ways to deliver health interventions, but the effectiveness of these methods varies across groups, and that the effectiveness of a particular interventionist may depend on the group to whom it is delivered.
